core.text: When you say *bigger by a lot* or *higher by ten feet*, the measure goes in the ablative: **the ablative of degree (the 'by how much' form: multo maior = bigger by much)**. *multō* (by much) and *paulō* (by a little) are the everyday ones: *terra multō pulchrior* — a land more beautiful by much, much more beautiful; *nāvis paulō levior fit* — the ship becomes a little lighter. Any measurement works: *decem pedibus altior* — ten feet higher. The ablative sits next to a comparative (the '-er / more' form) and says how far apart the two things are. Latin name: ablātīvus mēnsūrae.
English says *much bigger*, *ten feet higher*: the word before the *-er* form measures the gap. Latin puts that word in the ablative, which here means *by*.
multō / paulō / a measured amount, in the ablative, beside a comparative = 'by so much'.

invented.la: Frāter meus multō altior est quam ego.
invented.en: My brother is much taller than I am.

core.text: Two ablatives can stand near one comparative. *multō* answers *by how much?*; the ablative of comparison (the 'than' form: illo fortior = braver than he) answers *than whom?*. *Hic multō fortior est illō* — braver than that one (*illō*) by much (*multō*). A measure is degree; the thing compared is comparison.

more.text: The same ablative goes with words that hide a comparison, above all time words: *paulō post* — a little later; *multō ante* — long before; *paulō ante* — a little earlier (*quantī paulō ante* — as big as a little before). It also goes with *magis* (more) and *minus* (less): *multō magis laetābor* — I shall be much happier.
*tantō … quantō* — by so much … by how much: *quantō altior mōns, tantō frīgidior āēr* — the higher the mountain, the colder the air. *nihilō* (by nothing) makes *nihilō minus* — none the less.

Your notes: the ablative names the degree of difference between two things compared; it is either a unit of measure (*pēs* foot, *ūncia* inch, *passus* pace) or a general quantity word (*multum, paulum*); it can combine with a *quam* clause or with an ablative of comparison: *hic multō fortior est*, *hic multō fortior est illō*, *hī paulō māiōrēs sunt quam illī*, *mūrus decem pedibus altior est*. Ørberg (chapter XVI): *multō pulchriōrem, multō turbidior, multō altiōrēs, paulō levior*; A&G §414 call it the ablative of degree of difference.
